Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette:
Robert was a journalist who had built a career on bearing witness. For two decades, he had believed that if you just kept your eyes open, you could make sense of anything. That belief had shattered nine months ago in a dusty, windowless room. He had been on assignment, reporting on a regional conflict, when his car was stopped. The next three weeks were a blur of darkness, punctuated by moments of stark, unbearable clarity. Now, those moments were all that remained. He explained that the memory of it wasn't a story he could tell, but a film that played over and over in his mind, often without warning. It would force its way in when he was trying to write a deadline story or sitting at the dinner table with his wife, Sarah. Suddenly, he would be back on the cold concrete floor, the smell of cheap, sour liquor thick in the air from his captors' breath, the rough grip of a hand on the back of his neck forcing his head down. When the memory arrived, it wasn't a recollection; it was a recurrence. The same terror that had seized his lungs then would return with full force, leaving him breathless and trembling in his quiet suburban home.

The world outside that room had become a minefield. At 45, Robert had always been a social man, comfortable in crowds, quick with a story at a party. Now, he was constantly on guard, superalert to a threat he couldn't name but felt in his bones. The open-plan office of the newspaper where he worked, once a hub of collaborative energy, now felt like an arena of unpredictable dangers. An intern dropping a stack of papers would send a jolt of pure adrenaline through him; for a split second, he was certain it was the sound of a rifle bolt sliding home. He would react before he could think, ducking his head, his body tensing for an impact that never came. He knew, intellectually, that he was safe, but his body was convinced otherwise. This constant state of high alert made concentration impossible. He started missing deadlines, his once-sharp prose becoming muddled and hesitant. He began working from home, but the false alarms followed him there, triggered by a car backfiring on the street or a neighbour slamming a door.

His life at home had shrunk. The triggers were everywhere, insidious and specific. The sharp, persistent ache in his neck, a physical remnant of being held in stress positions, was a constant somatic reminder. On days when the pain flared, the intrusive "film" was more vivid, the terror more acute. He stopped going to friends' houses for dinner after an evening when a host opened a bottle of whiskey. The smell of the alcohol hit him like a physical blow, and he had to stumble outside, gasping for air, leaving Sarah to make his excuses. The most painful change, however, was in his marriage. Sarah's attempts to comfort him, a simple hand on his shoulder or an arm around his waist, felt like attacks. Any physical touch he didn't initiate sent a shockwave of panic through him. He would flinch away violently, sometimes pushing her hand away, the reflex faster than his love for her. He saw the hurt in her eyes, a confusion that was hardening into resentment. He had come to believe he was fundamentally broken, a danger even to those he loved. It was after a night when he woke up shouting from a nightmare and found Sarah sleeping on the sofa, her face etched with fear and exhaustion, that he finally made the call. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a desperate, fragmented plea: to stop the film, to be able to hold his wife's hand, and to feel safe in his own home again.
